name: Azul
lede: Azul is simply the Spanish and Portuguese word for blue, used here as the name of a saturated medium blue from a 2010 online color survey.

sections.title: A word for blue
sections.body:
*Azul* is the Spanish and Portuguese word for blue [1]. As a color name in our library it comes from the xkcd color survey of 2010, where it labels a strong, slightly violet blue close to [[royal-blue]] [3]. Our measured nearest named color is Royal Blue, 4.2 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [3].

The Pigment Compendium follows the family of words (Old French *azur*, Old Spanish *azur*, Spanish and Portuguese *azul*, Italian *azzurro*) back to Arabic and Persian words that are taken to mean lapis lazuli, the blue stone [2]. The initial *l* was dropped in the Romance languages, apparently along with the Arabic article, and that is the conventional view rather than a proven one [2]. It is also the route by which [[azure]] and [[lapis-lazuli]] share a root with *azul* [2].

sections.title: Azul in the pigment trade
sections.body:
Old pigment names show that *azul* was never one material. *Azul baxo* is cited, on the authority of Veliz, as a low grade of azurite, and it appears in the Spanish treatise of Carducho from 1633 [2]. *Cenizas de azul*, "blue ashes", is among the names for blue copper carbonate pigment, the verditer family [2]. *Azorium romanum* is listed as a historical term for [[indigo]] [2].

Across these entries the word names a blue, not one mineral or dye, so a buyer needed the grade and source to know what was in the pot [2].

sections.title: Blue blood
sections.body: Paterson explains the Spanish phrase *sangre azul* as pure Spanish ancestry with no Moorish blood [1]. Pastoureau, writing on whiteness, ties French blue blood to aristocrats keeping their skin pale to stand apart from sun-browned peasants [4]. The books give different stories, so treat each as a proposal rather than a settled origin.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Azul is a survey name, not a historic one, and our data reflects that. No painting among the 23,781 in our archive has this color across at least 1% of its canvas, as photographed [3]. That describes our archive of museum paintings, not painting as a whole.

Its nearest named neighbors are royal blue and [[cobalt-blue]], with [[cerulean]] on the lighter side [3].

openers: Azul, azure and lapis lazuli share one ancient root: the word for a blue stone.
In 1633 a Spanish treatise listed azul baxo, a low grade of azurite.
